title: 100 Things 1% Better
author: Begum, Thahmina
source: TB Blogs, CST T&L Bulletin (tbeeblogs.wordpress.com), June 12, 2023
summary: Thahmina Begum applies British Cycling's "aggregation of marginal gains," the strategy credited with turning the team from perennial underachievers into Olympic dominators under Dave Brailsford, to the granular mechanics of teaching, arguing that big CPD-style exhortations to "find your marginal gains" fail because they stay abstract. She makes the idea concrete by breaking down a single routine, dismissing a class, into thirteen discrete components, each of which could individually be refined by a small amount. Her argument leans on Parkinson's Law, that work expands to fill available time, to explain why teachers can't simply "find more time," and instead should treat their fixed time as a constraint to optimise within rather than a problem to solve. She closes with a direct challenge to the reader to identify which of the thirteen components of their own class-dismissal routine they've improved this year and which they could still refine by just 1%, framing marginal, unglamorous improvement as the realistic alternative to waiting for more time that will never arrive.
points: Begum's key reframe of marginal gains is specificity: rather than a vague CPD exhortation, she models it with a thirteen-component breakdown of one five-minute routine, showing what "concrete and super-specific" actually looks like in practice.
She uses Parkinson's Law explicitly to argue that "gained" time never actually produces more available time, reframing the goal from finding time to improving within fixed time.

Her quote from James Clear, that a 1% improvement "isn't particularly notable... but it can be far more meaningful, especially in the long run," is used to justify investing effort in improvements too small to notice day to day.
The piece's implicit argument against big, one-off CPD initiatives is that they tend to stay "abstract and gimmicky" unless broken down to the level of a specific, repeatable classroom routine.
quotes: Parkinson’s Law is the adage that work will expand to fill the time allotted for its completion. This plays out every year with ‘gain’ time from exam classes – it can seem like the only thing we gain is more work!

In Atomic Habits, James Clear uses the British cycling team to exemplify the idea of 100 things, 1% better. After hiring their new performance director, Dave Brailsford in 2003, the team went from winning just 1 gold medal in the last 100 years to winning 70% of the gold medals available in the 2012 Olympics.

He broke down the sport to every component he could think contributed to their performance and looked to improve each thing by 1%: from obvious things like changing tyres and wearing lighter cycling gear to less obvious things like learning to wash hands better to reduce the risk of getting ill and buying better pillows to improve the quality of the sleep of each rider.

Clear says, ‘improving by 1% isn’t particularly notable—sometimes it isn’t even noticeable—but it can be far more meaningful, especially in the long run. The difference a tiny improvement can make over time is astounding.

The goal of the British cycling team didn’t change. Nor did the time they had to achieve their goal. As teachers, our goal remains the same: being better in our practice every day so that our students get the best deal in their education.
